questions.text: What is the architect's liability if a building designed by the architect fails to meet BP 344 accessibility standards?

options.text: No liability exists, as the responsibility lies solely with the contractor and building owner
Professional negligence; architect is liable to affected PWDs, building owner, and potentially regulatory action
Only the contractor is liable, provided that the architect has fulfilled all design obligations and specifications
Liability cannot be established unless there is clear evidence of design oversight or non-compliance with BP 344

rationale.a: Dangerously incorrect; BP 344 violations create direct architect liability.
rationale.c: Misplaces liability; while contractors execute, architects designed the failure; architects bear design liability.
rationale.d: False; accessibility failures are clearly negligent and liability is well-established in Philippine law.
rationale.correct: Failure to meet BP 344 accessibility standards constitutes professional negligence; architects are liable to affected PWDs for damages, to building owners for non-compliance, and face potential regulatory action by DENR and disciplinary action by the Board of Architecture.
rationale.takeaway: Accessibility is non-negotiable—failure to meet BP 344 exposes architects to civil liability to PWDs, owner liability, and professional discipline.

questions.code_citation: BP 344; RA 7277; Code of Ethical Conduct

questions.text: At what design phase should accessibility be integrated?

options.text: Only during construction, when physical adjustments can be made
Conceptual phase onward, including site planning and building form decisions
Only in detailed design, focusing on specific elements like door widths and ramp slopes
After construction, if budget allows, to retrofit necessary features

rationale.a: Too late; construction-only accessibility integration cannot change fundamental site and building form decisions.
rationale.c: Too late; detailed design cannot fix site planning or building form errors; early integration prevents costly changes.
rationale.d: Dangerously wrong; waiting until after construction to address accessibility violates BP 344 and is impossible to retrofit economically.
rationale.correct: Accessibility must be integrated from the conceptual design phase onward because early decisions (site selection, building orientation, entry positioning) determine whether accessibility is possible.
rationale.takeaway: Accessibility cannot be retrofitted—it must be designed in from schematic phase to prevent costly redesigns later.

questions.text: Why is segregated access (separate elevators or entrances for PWDs) discouraged in modern accessibility practice?

options.text: It is less expensive, which can be a consideration in budget-constrained projects but does not align with inclusive design principles
It reduces design complexity, allowing for simpler layouts but failing to meet the needs of all users in an equitable manner
Universal Design philosophy favors integrated design where all persons use the same facilities; segregation implies discrimination
Segregated access is actually required by law, particularly in older buildings where retrofitting is not feasible

rationale.a: Misconception; segregated access may appear cheaper initially but reduces overall design quality.
rationale.b: Misconception; segregated access may seem simpler but contradicts accessibility standards requiring integration.
rationale.d: False; law permits segregated facilities but modern standards reject this approach in favor of integration.
rationale.correct: Modern accessibility philosophy rejects segregation; Universal Design dictates a single accessible main entrance, shared restrooms with accessible stalls, and integrated circulation—segregated facilities imply discrimination.
rationale.takeaway: Integrated accessible design (one main entrance for all, shared facilities) is the standard, not segregated back entrances for PWDs.

questions.text: What is the recommended ramp slope ratio according to BP 344?

options.text: 1:6 (steep), which may be used in exceptional cases with proper justification and safety measures
1:12 preferred, steeper allowed temporarily with conditions
1:20 (too shallow), generally not recommended for accessibility purposes
Any slope is acceptable if it meets the specific needs of the project and is approved by the relevant authorities

rationale.a: Too steep; 1:6 slope is dangerous for wheelchair and mobility device users and violates BP 344 standards.
rationale.c: 1:20 is maximum for temporary ramps per BP 344; 1:12 is maximum for permanent ramps.
rationale.d: False; BP 344 specifies precise ramp slopes; any slope without meeting standards violates accessibility requirements.
rationale.correct: BP 344 specifies maximum ramp slope of 1:12 (1V:12H) for permanent ramps; maximum 1:20 allowed temporarily with handrails and landings.
rationale.takeaway: Use 1:12 ramp slope; steeper slopes (e.g., 1:8) require additional handrails and landings and should only be temporary solutions.

options.text: Design that only works for disabled persons, focusing solely on accessibility features
Designing for all people regardless of ability; integrated access benefits everyone
Design that looks the same everywhere, lacking cultural or contextual adaptation
Expensive design for wealthy clients, often involving luxury materials and finishes

rationale.a: Misses the point; Universal Design benefits all people, not just PWDs.
rationale.c: Misses the philosophy; Universal Design allows variety while ensuring all people can access and use spaces.
rationale.d: False cost assumption; Universal Design is not inherently expensive and often requires no cost penalty.
rationale.correct: Universal Design means designing for all people regardless of ability; curb cuts help parents with strollers and delivery personnel, clear wayfinding helps elderly and visitors, accessible heights serve wheelchair users and short persons alike.
rationale.takeaway: Universal Design benefits everyone—curb cuts, clear signage, and accessible heights are not special accommodations, they improve design for all.

questions.text: What accessibility features should architects prioritize for persons with vision loss?

options.text: Only wheelchair ramps, as they are universally required for all disabilities
Contrast, tactile paving, Braille signage, adequate non-glare lighting, and hazard warnings
Loud announcements only, as auditory cues are sufficient for navigation
No special features are needed, as standard building designs are adequate

rationale.a: Incomplete; ramps serve mobility, not vision—vision accessibility requires tactile and visual cues.
rationale.c: Insufficient; announcements help hearing-based wayfinding but do not guide blind users through physical spaces.
rationale.d: False; persons with vision loss need designed features to navigate safely—adequate lighting, contrast, tactile guides, and signage are essential.
rationale.correct: Vision accessibility requires contrast (colors, textures), tactile paving at entries and hazards, Braille and tactile signage, adequate non-glare lighting for low-vision users, and contrasting-color handrails.
rationale.takeaway: For vision loss: use contrast, tactile guides, Braille signage, good lighting without glare, and hazard warnings—not just ramps.

questions.text: Which law reinforces PWD rights by establishing the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons?

rationale.a: Wrong law; RA 9184 governs government procurement.
rationale.b: Wrong law; RA 10173 is the Data Privacy Act.
rationale.d: Wrong law; RA 9266 is the Architecture Law regulating the profession.
rationale.correct: RA 7277 (Magna Carta for Disabled Persons) establishes that persons with disabilities have the same rights and responsibilities as all citizens.
rationale.takeaway: RA 7277 reinforces accessibility as a rights issue, not a charity—PWDs have equal participation rights in all public and private spaces.

questions.text: How should accessibility be verified during construction administration and after occupancy?

options.text: No verification is needed, as accessibility is assumed to be inherent in the design
During construction, verify ramp slopes, handrail heights, door swings, and fixture installation; after occupancy, conduct post-occupancy review confirming accessible features remain functional
Only post-occupancy review is required, focusing on user feedback and accessibility audits
Accessibility never needs verification, as it is not a critical component of building design

rationale.a: Negligent approach; without verification, construction errors go undetected and accessible features may not function.
rationale.c: Incomplete; post-occupancy verification alone misses construction errors that occur during building.
rationale.d: False; verification is part of professional responsibility to ensure BP 344 compliance.
rationale.correct: Architects must verify during construction that accessible features are built as detailed (ramp slopes, handrail heights, door widths, fixture locations) and conduct post-occupancy review to confirm accessible features remain functional and unobstructed.
rationale.takeaway: Verify accessibility during construction and after occupancy—accessible features that are detailed correctly but built wrong, or built right but later blocked, still fail.

questions.text: What is the primary legal mandate for accessibility in the Philippines?

options.text: Board of Architecture preference, which is advisory rather than mandatory
Client request only, which may vary depending on project scope
Batas Pambansa Bilang 344 (Accessibility Law) requires accessible design for all new construction
Accessibility is optional for all projects, unless specified by local ordinances

rationale.a: Confuses accessibility with professional preference; BP 344 is a legal mandate, not a guideline.
rationale.b: Confuses accessibility with contractual option; BP 344 requires accessibility regardless of client request.
rationale.d: False legal statement; BP 344 makes accessibility mandatory for new construction with no general cost-based exemptions.
rationale.correct: BP 344 2024 Revised IRR (Accessibility Law) mandates that all new construction and alterations provide accessible facilities enabling persons with disabilities to access and use buildings.
rationale.takeaway: BP 344 is a mandatory legal requirement, not optional—accessibility is the default expectation for all new construction.

questions.text: What must be documented in contract documents to ensure accessibility compliance during construction?

options.text: General notes only, as they provide a broad overview of compliance requirements without detailing specific elements
Explicit accessibility features, dimensions, materials, ramp slopes, door swings, grab bar mounting, and signage specifications
No detail is needed, as accessibility compliance is assumed to be inherent in the design process
Only the cost estimate, which should reflect the inclusion of accessibility features without specifying them

rationale.a: Insufficient; general notes lead to construction errors; explicit detailed specifications are required.
rationale.c: Dangerously incorrect; without detailed specifications, contractors cannot build accessible features correctly.
rationale.d: Incomplete; cost estimates are not specifications—detailed drawings and specs are needed to guide construction.
rationale.correct: Contract documents must explicitly note all accessible features, dimensions, materials, ramp slopes, door widths, grab bar heights and mounting, and signage requirements—vague notes invite construction errors.
rationale.takeaway: Accessibility must be detailed in drawings and specifications—a ramp drawn to proper slope but built wrong still fails accessibility; detail prevents errors.
